newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Pyongyang sets out conditions for peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Pyongyang sets out conditions for peace talks.

text.p: North Korea signalled on Thursday it was seeking U.S. diplomatic recognition, large-scale food aid and an easing of trade sanctions before joining peace talks.
The conditions were hinted at by North Korea's top negotiator on the peace talks issue in comments carried by the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).
South Korea's Yonhap news agency quoted a Pyongyang official as saying until these conditions were met, North Korea would oppose participation by China in the talks.
Four-way peace talks between the two Koreas, the United States and China were proposed a year ago by U.S. President Bill Clinton and South Korean President Kim Young-sam.
The aim is to replace a now-ragged truce that halted the 1950-53 Korean War with a permanent peace arrangement.
"It is our stand to hold 'four-way talks' for peace and security of the Korean peninsula," Kim Kye-gwan was quoted as saying by KCNA.

But Kim urged the United States to adopt more confidence-building measures, in an apparent reference to famine-stricken North Korea's demands for substantial food aid and an end to sweeping U.S. economic sanctions.
He also suggested North Korea's lack of diplomatic relations with Washington was a stumbling block.
"Confidence needed for 'four-way talks' has not yet been built between the DPRK (North Korea) and the U.S. and, still worse, our equal footing at the talks has not been guaranteed," said Kim.

It was North Korea's first public comment since South Korean representatives returned from New York on Tuesday after tortuous negotiations failed to secure a clear-cut answer from Pyongyang on whether it was ready to enter peace talks.
Pyongyang agreed in principle to join the talks but set conditions. Washington and Seoul insist the talks should focus on peace, not diplomatic ties or food.
"The purpose of these meetings is not rice," said Seoul foreign ministry spokesman Lee Kyu-hyung. "They are trying to twist the real purpose of the talks.
"China will absolutely, automatically attend these meetings," he added.
Kim made clear the dialogue was not over.

"In order to make the talks more effective and productive, we proposed to have more rounds of negotiations among the DPRK, the United States and South Korea before beginning the 'four-way talks'," he said.
Yonhap quoted Han Song-yol, a senior official at North Korea's U.N. mission, as saying Pyongyang had proposed China drop out of peace talks until the conditions were met.

"China should join after North Korea's legal and political status is settled, and when the involved parties start gaining confidence about the four-party talks," Yonhap quoted Han as saying in an interview.
Meanwhile, the head of the South Korean Red Cross again proposed a meeting with his Northern counterpart in the border village of Panmunjom to discuss speeding up food aid.
The North Korean Red Cross welcomed Kang Young-hoon's original offer last week but suggested Beijing as a venue.

"I don't think there is any reason for North and South Korean Red Cross members to meet in another country," a Red Cross statement quoted Kang as saying in a message relayed across the border via a telephone "hot line".
Kang proposed a working-level meeting in Panmunjom next Tuesday.
